title: Teams ClickFix to a Sideloaded Backdoor and rclone Exfiltration
subtitle: A fake help desk on Teams, a pasted one-liner, a signed app with a patched DLL, and 2.7 GB uploaded with rclone seven hours later.

nodes.label: Fake help desk on Teams
nodes.sub: External account messages the user 7 min before
nodes.desc: An external account posing as the help desk messaged the user about seven minutes before the command ran. Just before the paste the user ran two net group /dom lookups in PowerShell, which looks like live coaching.
nodes.notes: The coaching is inference: we have alert data, not the chat.

nodes.label: PowerShell paste
nodes.sub: One-liner downloads a ZIP and runs the MSI inside
nodes.desc: The pasted one-liner downloads Secure-PDFDiamond.zip, unpacks it, runs the MSI with msiexec and deletes the ZIP. The MSI writes 23 executables and DLLs to a FileLocator Index Manager folder and launches the signed IndexManager.exe.

nodes.label: Signed app, patched DLL
nodes.sub: IndexManager.exe loads a DLL patched after signing
nodes.desc: ConfigUILib.dll is a genuine vendor DLL patched after signing to import apiModel.dll. Its recomputed Authenticode digest doesn't match its signature, while IndexManager.exe and SearchLib.dll do.
nodes.notes: High for the files. I have no image-load event for the runtime load, so that half stays assessed.

nodes.label: Payload in a WAV file
nodes.sub: XOR-decoded shellcode, run after a 62 s wait
nodes.desc: apiModel.dll starts a thread on load, reads 341,475 bytes from offset 0x30cea of LibraryPipelines.wav, XOR-decodes them, sleeps 62 seconds, and runs the result from an RWX buffer by passing it to EnumSystemCodePagesW as a callback. Reproducing the decoder in Python turned entropy 7.39 into x64 code.

nodes.label: Script sets persistence
nodes.sub: Run key and task on timers, then loads the implant
nodes.desc: The decoded blob opens Compress.db, a custom container of 1,128 entries whose main entry is a script. It re-creates the Run key every 150 seconds and the task every 875 seconds, then loads the real implant, a 1.58 MB blob. Both entries point at the host process, so every restart re-runs the sideload.
nodes.notes: Medium: the Run key at T+4 and the task at T+16 match the script's timers, but that is a timing match, not a log of the script firing.

nodes.label: Defender block at T+5
nodes.sub: Persistence blocked once; the loop puts it back
nodes.desc: Defender blocked a persistence behavior at T+5 (low severity), yet the backdoor was back at the next sign-in. The script's loops explain why persistence survived the block.

nodes.label: HTTPS C2, DoH lookups
nodes.sub: IndexManager.exe connects out at T+2 min
nodes.desc: Two minutes after install the process connected out over HTTPS and queried a public DNS-over-HTTPS resolver directly, bypassing the organization's DNS logs. The implant matches public reporting on the CNCMachineRMS framework.
nodes.notes: The C2 address comes from telemetry; I never recovered the gate from the binaries. High for family, nothing for an actor.

nodes.label: rclone to IDrive e2
nodes.desc: Six quiet hours later a shell ran net use, net view against a file server and ipconfig /all, and the host process wrote rclone.exe into the user's Music folder. The commands were stock rclone: config create for an IDrive e2 remote, then copy with --include filters. Defender's DLP telemetry named 334 files, 32 tagged as exfiltrated; given the byte count I treat all 334 as sent.
nodes.notes: Open: the exact file list (the file server's audit log is the authority) and whether the copy was downloaded elsewhere.

nodes.label: Alert, then isolation
nodes.sub: High alert in the same second; isolated at T+7 h 36
nodes.desc: The first rclone run raised a high-severity exfiltration alert in the same second and Defender stopped it three minutes on. The operator swapped in a renamed build, iclone.exe, which Defender flagged for its mismatched original filename, then a second one. The SOC isolated the host 36 minutes after the first high-severity alert.
